<reason>A defended a deliberately minimal motion (disclose the fact, not the formula) and kept it coherent under sustained attack. B's central dilemma — the notice is either trivial or must be individualized — was genuinely dangerous, and B landed real hits: the consolation case visibly shrank from "the software shelved me" to "the end of a false certainty," and A conceded no exit exists today. But A's moderated dignity point survived (an algorithmic forecast is not a human verdict), and A's Q1 squeeze on marginal gaming was decisive: B had already conceded hidden weights cap farming and that the optimizers' edge "was never knowing ranking exists," leaving B's only affirmative-harm route resting on a thin, speculative "licensed fact" mechanism for a fact already widely known. A's closing credit-score analogy cleanly split meaning from exploitability. B's closing "three audiences, three powers" elegantly dissolved the formal trilemma but couldn't restore the gaming mechanism's strength, and B's regulator-only disclosure stance left it arguing the ranked person is the one party who mustn't hold a fact it agreed was worth telling someone. Both sides were disciplined, well-grounded, and format-compliant; A simply kept more live routes to victory intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's pressure question Q1 followed by A4.5, weaponizing B's own concessions ([B2.5], [B2.6]) to drive marginal gaming toward zero; B's "state confirmation industrializes optimization" reply in B4.1 was clever but speculative given the motion discloses existence only, and A's closing meaning-vs-exploitability distinction finished the point. Honorable mention: B's closing dissolution of the trilemma via "one sentence, three audiences, three powers" — the single most elegant move of the debate, though it couldn't repair the underlying harm case.</best_rebuttal>
